name: Spearmint tea

card.summary: A herbal tea said to lower androgens and calm hormonal acne; one small trial studied androgens in PCOS, and none tested acne.
card.note: The human research is on androgens and hirsutism in PCOS, not on acne.

quick.overview:
Spearmint tea is an infusion of the leaves of Mentha spicata, a common culinary herb [1]. In skin-care and hormonal-acne circles it is promoted as a mild anti-androgen drink that could reduce oil and breakouts.
The human research behind the idea is a small randomized trial in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and excess hair growth, which examined anti-androgen effects [2]. A review of plant-derived anti-androgens discusses acne as one condition where such agents are of interest [3]. No trial tests spearmint tea on acne.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say compounds in spearmint lower circulating androgens such as testosterone, which drive sebum production. The PCOS trial title reports significant anti-androgen effects from the tea [2]; how this works and whether it reaches skin is not established.
quick.risks: Spearmint is a common food flavouring and tea ingredient [1]. No safety data specific to regular medicinal use of the tea exist.

lead: Spearmint tea is made by steeping the leaves of spearmint (Mentha spicata), a perennial herb native to Europe and southern temperate Asia that is widely used as a flavouring and in teas such as Maghrebi mint tea [1].

In wellness and skin-care communities it is promoted as an anti-androgen drink for hormonal acne and for hirsutism. The research most often cited is a randomized controlled trial of spearmint herbal tea in women with PCOS, reported in 2010 in Phytotherapy Research, whose title states significant anti-androgen effects [2]. That paper itself notes that it set out to test whether lowering androgens translates to clinical improvement in hirsutism, a question earlier work had not addressed [2].

A 2012 review of plant-derived anti-androgens lists acne alongside PCOS, hirsutism and prostate conditions as areas where reducing androgen activity matters, and discusses the growing recognition of plant-based options [3]. No human trial tests spearmint tea for acne.

paras: Spearmint leaves are steeped in hot water to make tea; the herb's main aroma compound is carvone, and the leaves and oil are also used in food, toothpaste and confectionery [1].

Spearmint grows 30 to 100 cm tall from spreading rhizomes, with serrated leaves and pink or white flower spikes; the name refers to its pointed leaf tips [1]. References to it date back at least to the first century AD, and Wikipedia notes the Romans brought it to England and that it was a cash crop in Connecticut during the American Revolution, when untaxed mint tea was popular [1]. It is the mint in Maghrebi mint tea, and also flavours cocktails such as the mojito, Southern US sweet tea and, in Western Australia, spearmint milk [1]. Its oil is rich in carvone with little menthol, which distinguishes it from peppermint [1].

Advocates of the tea say a daily cup or two can lower androgens and thereby reduce oily skin, hormonal acne and unwanted facial hair. The idea rests on the PCOS trial and on a broader literature on plant anti-androgens [2][3].

The study usually cited is a two-centre randomised controlled trial published in 2010. Forty-two volunteers with PCOS-related hirsutism drank spearmint tea twice a day for a month and were compared with a placebo herbal tea; 41 completed it. Hormones and gonadotrophins were measured at 0, 15 and 30 days, hirsutism was rated clinically with the Ferriman-Galwey score, and a modified Dermatology Quality of Life Index captured self-reported hirsutism [2]. The authors reported significant falls in free and total testosterone in the spearmint group, increases in LH and FSH, and lower self-rated hirsutism scores on the questionnaire [2]. The paper says it built on earlier research in Turkey showing anti-androgenic properties of spearmint tea in women with hirsutism [2].

A 2012 review of plant-derived anti-androgens lists spearmint tea in PCOS as a case where some evidence of efficacy is beginning to emerge, alongside red reishi and green tea (5-alpha-reductase inhibition), licorice, Chinese peony, black cohosh and chaste tree [3]. A 2026 narrative review of beverages and skin health concludes that spearmint tea lowers free testosterone in women with PCOS, though objective clinical benefit remains unproven, and notes that for green tea the randomised acne data favour topical extract rather than drinking it [4].

The 2010 trial was a two-centre, 30-day randomized controlled study in women with PCOS-related hirsutism, built on earlier research from Turkey suggesting anti-androgenic properties of spearmint tea [2]. A review of plant-derived anti-androgens describes the use of anti-androgen medicines in PCOS, hirsutism, acne and other conditions and surveys plant-derived alternatives [3]. A 2026 review in Clinics in Dermatology covers dietary beverages and skin health for dermatologists [4]. Other spearmint studies found in searches covered unrelated topics, such as knee osteoarthritis symptoms and antimutagenic activity in bacterial assays [5][6].

Spearmint's other studied properties include rosmarinic-acid content, tested in a 16-week knee osteoarthritis trial [5], and inhibition of mutagen activation in Salmonella assays by brewed leaf water extracts [6]. In that assay, the tea extract blocked the mutagenic activity of one heterocyclic compound in a concentration-dependent way and inhibited cytochrome P450 1A1 and 1A2 enzymes [6]. These are not appearance studies.

No studies found on spearmint tea for acne. The closest human evidence is a 30-day randomized controlled trial in women with PCOS-related hirsutism that assessed anti-androgen effects [2]. Spearmint tea has also been studied in knee osteoarthritis in a randomized double-blind trial of 62 participants over 16 weeks, which is unrelated to appearance [5].

In the PCOS trial, 42 women were randomised, 41 completed 30 days, and free and total testosterone fell significantly in the spearmint group (p below 0.05) [2]. In the knee osteoarthritis trial, 62 participants were randomised to high-rosmarinic-acid spearmint tea or commercial spearmint for 16 weeks; 46 were analysed, and pain scores fell within the high-rosmarinic group but between-group differences were not significant [5].

timeline.event: A randomized controlled trial of spearmint tea in women with PCOS reports anti-androgen effects [2].
A review of plant-derived anti-androgens is published [3].

lore.intro: Spearmint tea circulates in hormonal-acne and skin-care discussions as a food-based anti-androgen; the claims below come from how the research is typically cited [2][3].

claims.believers: Proponents point to the PCOS trial, whose title reports significant anti-androgen effects from drinking the tea [2].
claims.experts: The trial was small and short (30 days), and it concerns women with PCOS; reviews of plant anti-androgens treat the area as emerging [2][3].

claims.believers: Advocates reason that lower androgens should mean less sebum and fewer breakouts, extending the PCOS findings to acne [3].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested spearmint tea on acne.

angle.text: People drink spearmint tea as a food-based anti-androgen, hoping lower androgen activity will mean fewer hormonal breakouts and less unwanted facial hair. The human data that exist concern women with polycystic ovary syndrome and hirsutism, where blood testosterone fell over 30 days.
